## The third surface

The simplification epic has censused this CLI carefully and twice. Both censuses counted the same two surfaces:

| surface | measured | contracted | governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| commands | 77 | yes (`pm contracts`) | `pm-n7rr` noun grammar, `pm-wt43zj` gate |
| flags | 1,712 declarations / 470 spellings | yes (`*_FLAG_CONTRACTS`) | `pm-fs8q9x` lexicon + budget |
| **error codes** | **195** | **no** | **nothing** |

Measured 2026-07-26 on the shipped 2026.7.26 build: `grep -rhoE 'code: "[a-z_]+"' src/ --include=*.ts | sort -u | wc -l` returns **195**. `pm contracts --json | jq keys` returns fourteen keys — `actions`, `commands`, `command_aliases`, `governance_contracts`, `runtime_schema`, and others — and none of them enumerates an error code. Grepping `docs/` for a representative code (`item_not_found`) returns nothing.

So the surface an agent hits when it is *wrong* — the surface it reads most carefully, under the most pressure, and the one this repository invests most in making structured — is the only one of the three that an agent cannot enumerate in advance.

## What follows from that, concretely

- **Handlers cannot be pre-written.** An integration that wants to branch on "the item is locked by another agent" versus "the item does not exist" has to discover `lock_conflict` and `item_not_found` by triggering them. At a thousand-agent fleet, that is a lot of deliberate failure.
- **Stability is unstated.** Nothing declares whether a code is permanent. `pm-e6tm5c` freezes the SDK export surface and `pnpm contracts:check` freezes the command/flag contracts; a code can be renamed in a patch release with no gate objecting, which quietly breaks every consumer that branched on it.
- **The taxonomy cannot be reviewed.** 195 codes across 94 CLI files is well past the size where a human notices that two codes mean the same thing. Duplicates and near-synonyms are invisible without an enumeration, which is exactly the argument `pm-fs8q9x` makes for flags ("one spelling per concept") applied to a vocabulary three times as large as the flag vocabulary it is compared against here.
- **Exit codes carry almost no information.** Source declares `exit_code: 0` and `exit_code: 1` as literals; the richer values observed at runtime (`2` for usage, `3` for not-found) come from elsewhere. Nothing maps the 195 codes onto that small integer set as a documented contract, so a shell consumer that can only see `$?` has no documented way to classify a failure.

## Why this belongs to the simplification epic rather than beside it

The epic's thesis is that agents are paying too much to learn this CLI. It has been measured against the noun count and the flag count. Reducing 77 nouns to 12 while leaving 195 undocumented error codes simplifies the happy path and leaves the recovery path exactly as expensive as it was — and the recovery path is where agents spend tokens they did not plan for.

The two defects found in the same session as this census make the point without hypotheticals: `pm-yqe0mo` (a recovery hint that silently truncates its candidate list to three of six) and `pm-cyrfjq` (mode-paired envelopes that zero-fill the inactive key). Neither would have shipped if the error and envelope surface were enumerated and reviewed as a contract, because both are visible the moment you look at the surface as a whole rather than one command at a time.

## Deliverable

- An error-code catalog in `pm contracts`, generated from the same declarations the runtime uses, so it cannot drift from reality. Each entry carries: code, stable exit code, whether the code is stable or provisional, the commands that can emit it, and a one-line meaning.
- A snapshot gate in the shape already used by `contracts:check` and `sdk:surface:check`: adding a code is a reviewed change, renaming or removing a stable code fails the build.
- A deduplication pass over the 195, applying `pm-fs8q9x`'s one-spelling-per-concept rule to codes. Near-synonyms are merged behind aliases rather than deleted, matching the alias-preserving policy the grammar ADR already established for commands.
- A documented mapping from code class to exit code, so `$?` alone classifies a failure for shell consumers, satisfying the part of `pm-psy1`'s scripting contract that concerns exit codes.
- The catalog is emitted under a tier so it does not inflate the default `pm contracts` payload, which is itself a token-budgeted surface.

## Relationship to neighbours

- `pm-n7rr` owns the surface census. This item extends the census to its third dimension and is scoped as a child of the same epic.
- `pm-fs8q9x` establishes one spelling per concept and a per-command flag budget. The same rule applied to a 195-entry vocabulary is this item's deduplication pass; the two should share a checker rather than build two.
- `pm-185870` unifies the unknown-subcommand error across families. That is one code done well; this is the enumeration that would show which other codes need the same treatment.
- `pm-psy1` owns the scripting contract's exit-code guarantees. The code-to-exit-code mapping is the data that contract needs and does not currently have.
- `pm-cha95z` budgets diagnostic output. A catalog makes it possible to budget per code class rather than per command.
- `pm-yqe0mo` and `pm-cyrfjq` are the two concrete escapes that motivate the enumeration; both are recorded as `discovered_from` neighbours of the same review.
- `pm-e6tm5c` (closed) is the precedent for the gate shape: a reviewed snapshot of a public surface with a breaking-change check.
The CLI has 195 error codes and contracts none of them: the surface agents read when they are wrong is the only one with no enumeration, no stability promise, and no gate

Measured 2026-07-26: 195 distinct error codes declared across src, zero present in pm contracts (fourteen keys, none an error catalog) and zero documented in docs. Commands (77) and flags (470 spellings) are both contracted and gated; the third surface is not. Consumers must trigger failures to discover codes, a code can be renamed in a patch with no gate objecting, and 195 codes across 94 files cannot be deduplicated without an enumeration. Duplicate check 2026-07-26: searched error-code/taxonomy/contracts/exit-code items across all statuses; pm-185870 unifies one code family, pm-psy1 owns exit-code guarantees, pm-fs8q9x owns flag lexicon. No item enumerates or gates the error vocabulary.

pm contracts emits an error-code catalog generated from the same declarations the runtime uses, so it cannot drift; each entry carries code, stable exit code, stable-or-provisional status, emitting commands, and a one-line meaning; a snapshot gate in the shape of contracts:check and sdk:surface:check makes adding a code a reviewed change and makes renaming or removing a stable code fail the build; a deduplication pass applies the one-spelling-per-concept rule from pm-fs8q9x to the 195 codes, merging near-synonyms behind aliases rather than deleting them; a documented code-class to exit-code mapping lets a shell consumer classify a failure from exit status alone, closing the exit-code half of pm-psy1; the catalog is emitted under a surface tier so the default pm contracts payload does not grow
The error vocabulary becomes an enumerated, tiered, stability-tagged contract that agents can read before they fail instead of after

Integrations pre-write handlers instead of discovering codes by deliberate failure; a renamed code fails the build instead of breaking consumers silently; the vocabulary becomes reviewable and therefore deduplicable

The simplification epic has censused commands and flags twice and never counted error codes; two independent defects in exactly this surface were found in the same review, both of a kind that an enumeration would have exposed on sight

value.text:
A misclassification instance for the catalog, build 2026.7.29.

Running workspace snapshot restore with an empty target produces this envelope: type urn:pm-cli:error:unknown_error, code unknown_error, title "Unhandled error", detail "Snapshot names and fingerprints must use lowercase letters, digits, dots, underscores, or hyphens", exit_code 1, why "Unexpected runtime failures can occur from environment or extension-level issues", examples pm --help and pm health --json.

The detail is precise and correct - it names a declared input grammar. Everything around it is wrong for the situation: the code says the failure was unexpected, the why blames the environment or an extension, and the recovery examples point at root help and a health check instead of the one command that would supply a valid target, workspace snapshot list.

The generalisable rule this argues for, alongside the catalog and stability work already in scope here: no violation of a declared input grammar may surface under an unknown or unhandled code. That is checkable as a negative control - feed each documented grammar a deliberately invalid value and assert the emitted code is a typed input error - which makes it a cheap conformance test rather than a review habit.
